title: A new Ceremony workspace
question: Choose the replacement design. Authentication behavior and reusable components stay intact.

options.label: Connection workbench
options.lineage: Request workbenches and instrument control panels
options.thesis: The active authentication step is the workspace, not a card below a marketing headline.
options.viewport: A compact connector rail, large central auth workspace and quiet permissions column, with the primary action visible immediately.
options.risk: Too much status detail would distract users; only the current step and requested permissions deserve prominence.

raised.raise: Show only the current actionable step; never imply every protocol shares the same number of steps.
Selection must change the whole active context, not merely recolor a tile.
Keep method explanations aligned in a readable supporting column.
Controls need unmistakable pressed and focused states without decorative textures.
Make each status label own exactly one verified fact.
Keep authoring and running a template one deliberate navigation step apart.

options.label: Permission review
options.lineage: Permission review sheets and account settings
options.thesis: One service, one clearly explained authorization decision, one primary action.
options.viewport: A horizontal service selector above one broad review sheet; method choices left, current fields and permissions right.
options.risk: Familiar and effective, but close to conventional account-settings design.

options.label: Fold sequence
options.thesis: Authentication unfolds as successive reversible panels.
options.viewport: One current action centered in a sequence of folded panels.
options.risk: A physical fold metaphor suggests reversibility that external authorization cannot guarantee.
options.case: Less recognizable to integration developers and less precise about protocol state than the workbench.

options.label: Rain garden
options.thesis: Connector methods converge into a common completion destination.
options.viewport: Methods surround a central active flow.
options.risk: Spatial routing competes with reading and keyboard completion.
options.case: The audience does not need a physics metaphor and it obscures the next required action.

options.label: Auth lexicon
options.thesis: Methods are entries with explanatory margin notes.
options.viewport: A typographic methods index and a broad active entry.
options.risk: Reads as protocol documentation rather than a task interface.
options.case: Book apparatus is less familiar than a workbench and weakens action hierarchy.

options.label: Connection folio
options.thesis: Each connector is a physical account folio.
options.viewport: A shelf of services opens an account page.
options.risk: Material simulation dominates the protocol interaction.
options.case: Neither developer identification nor action clarity improves over the workbench.

options.label: Night instruments
options.thesis: Independent instruments report auth state and permissions.
options.viewport: A fixed status constellation surrounds the active action.
options.risk: Gauges imply numerical measurements the ceremony does not have.
options.case: Instrument monitoring is less relevant and less clear than completing the current step.

options.label: Ceremony stack
options.thesis: Browse and author share a black-and-white stack of ceremony screens.
options.viewport: One editable auth screen with a visible return path.
options.risk: Retro chrome distracts from contemporary native controls.
options.case: The authoring connection is useful, but retro conventions weaken identification and auth clarity.
options.kept: Short path between authoring and execution.

canonCard.label: Standard integration dashboard
canonCard.thesis: A familiar service directory and connection dialog.
canonCard.viewport: Service cards fill the workspace; selecting one opens its auth form.
